summary:
Amasya stands under the national framework of Türkiye, and the record contains no Amasya-specific provision, ordinance or enforcement finding. The province-specific layer of this assessment is therefore empty: what a trans visitor faces in Amasya is the country-wide regime described below, applied without any documented local mitigation or local aggravation.

A leaked draft of Türkiye's omnibus '11th Judicial Package', reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025, would open the way to criminal charges against LGBT people. Human Rights Watch called it one of the most alarming rollbacks of rights in decades. Conduct deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality', including its so-called 'promotion', would carry up to three years in prison; participation in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony would carry up to four years, and since same-sex marriage is not legal in Türkiye such ceremonies are by definition symbolic. The draft would also restrict gender-affirming care, raising the surgery age from 18 to 25 and requiring permanent infertility as a condition, with medical professionals fined or imprisoned for up to seven years and transgender patients facing up to three years for care falling outside the new limits. Human Rights Watch assessed that the restrictions would push transition care into underground settings.

The draft had not been enacted when reported, but its pending status has not stopped authorities from behaving as though equivalent prohibitions already bind them. Kaos GL's 2025 report, 'A Major Siege against LGBTI+ People in 2025: Hostility Turned into State Policy', documents hostility institutionalised under a 'Year of the Family' banner, with instructions issued to public institutions and hate speech from senior officials, alongside censored broadcasts and cancelled artistic events. The report presents this as national practice, not as a choice made by any one province.

Kaos GL counted six right-to-life violations in 2025, three of them recorded as hate-motivated killings, with transgender people the most affected. These figures were compiled from media and civil-society reporting because the Turkish state keeps no official hate-crime statistics, so the true total cannot be verified from official sources.

The same report records 89 torture or ill-treatment violations, up from 51 the previous year, mostly linked to peaceful assembly; 336 violations of assembly rights; and 313 violations of liberty, a roughly 2.5-fold increase made up largely of detentions. It also documents event-specific bans and violent police attacks on peaceful gatherings.

Checkpoint contact is the principal routine risk for a foreign visitor. Türkiye requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. Police stops of trans women for 'General Information Gathering' (GBT) background checks have been recorded in Istanbul in 2025, with those stopped required to produce original documents; any such interaction is an occasion on which a passport can be compared against presentation, creating a direct outing risk where the two do not match.

Trans prisoners are placed by registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025, and the case was raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025, confirming that a trans man had been held in a women's prison and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added 'gender reassignment' as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the 'other' option and required e-reports to be issued, risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to care.
tangentialFactors:
The Istanbul cases cited above function as evidence of the national pattern rather than as a local rule: monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

Legal experts cited in reporting on the 2025 GBT stops argue that such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights, to which Türkiye is a party. That argument is contested at the level of advocacy and has not been shown to deter the practice.

The asymmetry of state response to violence is documented in individual cases. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest. Activists treat that detention asymmetry as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Human Rights Watch's 2008 report 'We Need a Law for Liberation', drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. It predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited as historical evidence of the regime's depth, not as a statement of current law.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Türkiye, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners.
localsOnly:
Turkish nationals and residents face the domestic side of the same regime: Kaos GL's 2025 counts of liberty and assembly violations were drawn overwhelmingly from detentions of residents at protests and Pride-related events, where event-specific bans and police force have been applied.

The Health Ministry's September 2025 regulation and the Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular change how gender-related care is recorded for people using the Turkish health system, removing the 'other' option from hospital records and routing documentation through mandatory e-reports.

Prison administration operates on a binary, heteronormative basis with no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints procedures are ineffective and can attract further violence, according to the Prison Insider profile prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association.

Human rights organisations coordinated from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation into the death of the trans prisoner Poyraz; accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Amasya-specific source appears in the inventory. Whether Amasya police conduct GBT-style stops, how the province's health authorities handle gender-related documentation, and whether any local tolerance or hostility departs from the national pattern are unresolved and not sourced here.

As of the October 2025 reporting, the '11th Judicial Package' was a leaked draft and had not been passed; its current legislative status is unresolved in this record. Enforcement under analogous provisions has been reported at national level, but no court judgment applying the draft's specific penalties is sourced.

Türkiye keeps no official hate-crime statistics, so the 2025 counts of right-to-life and hate-motivated killings rest on media and civil-society compilation and cannot be reconciled against state data.

Whether the Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025 has been formally published in full text, and its precise scope for foreign patients paying privately, are not established by the sources cited.
